metadata.title: PISA For Development Technical Strand A (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD technical strand paper is not an empirical student-level analysis of PISA microdata with a fitted predictive model; instead, it reviews technical issues for enhancing PISA cognitive instruments for developing countries. It discusses PISA’s standard test design features (rotated booklet design, trained administrators, and a questionnaire component) and the psychometric scaling approach used in PISA (Rasch-family multidimensional random coefficients implemented in ACER ConQuest). Because no analytic dataset with an explicit analytic sample and no model-based estimation with survey weights is reported here, student/sampling weights and replicate-weight procedures are not applicable to the paper’s reported outputs. For any future field trial or main survey analysis, analysts should follow PISA Technical Standards for sampling, translation/adaptation, and scaling/equating, and apply the complex survey design weights provided in the PISA data products when estimating population-representative statistics.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because this document is a technical framework and instrument-development review rather than an empirical analysis predicting PV-based achievement outcomes. The paper focuses on item pool targeting, cross-cultural validity, test design options, and scaling model fit considerations, without reporting a PV-based dependent variable or an estimation pipeline that would require PV combination rules. Missing-data handling is also not reported because no student-level analytic dataset with missingness mechanisms is analyzed in this paper.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level analytic sample is defined in this technical strand paper. The document synthesizes technical evidence from prior PISA administrations (notably PISA 2012) and uses item-pool and scaling information (e.g., Rasch-family scaling of PISA items and comparisons of item information functions to proficiency distributions) rather than estimating model parameters on a filtered microdata subset. Where country-level proficiency-level distributions are shown (e.g., PISA 2012 tables), they are presented as published descriptive results rather than as an analytic subsample created by the authors.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD technical strand paper (Strand A: Enhancement of PISA Cognitive Instruments) identifies technical issues for adapting PISA reading, mathematics, and science instruments to developing-country contexts without developing new cognitive items. It reviews the existing secure item pool (517 items used across PISA 2000–2012; 337 secure items) and shows that item difficulty targeting and item-by-country interactions (country DIF) can be large, threatening cross-country construct comparability. The paper discusses test design constraints (rotated booklet design, domain coverage, item formats, and administration logistics) and evaluates options such as omitting more difficult items, using fewer booklets, and conducting equating studies to document comparability. It also reviews PISA proficiency levels and argues that current described levels—especially at the lower end—may be insufficiently informative for many partner countries, suggesting complementary approaches such as reading components or new lower-difficulty items in future phases. No predictive ML model is estimated; the outputs are technical recommendations and psychometric design considerations.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction targets an official assessment framework, user guide, or technical manual without an empirical ML study. Sample sizes, ML algorithms, and predictive findings are intentionally null or empty per schema rules for non-empirical IEA/OECD documentation.
